description:
We are engineers. Selma, Rand, Mariam, and Batoul, interested in ML and app development 

We're building Nominal (Python/Streamlit), a mobile-friendly game where players design satellites to solve Omani environmental challenges (floods, agriculture, dust) by balancing budget, power, and orbit to match real NASA missions.

Why Join Us? Clear 48-hour scope, high local impact, and a strong demo.Seeking: Python/UI designers, Earth science enthusiasts, and Arabic speakers for Omani school outreach.
summary:
Nominal is a story-driven web game that teaches students aged 13+ how a space mission is designed, using real problems from Oman. Players help Noor, a girl from Sur, build a satellite for her school’s competition. With a 100-point budget, they choose a rocket, instruments, orbit, solar panels and antenna, and every choice has a trade-off in cost, mass, power, data and detail. If the design doesn’t fit, the launch is cancelled. Once in orbit, players handle real-world problems like solar storms, space debris and ground station outages.

Each of the four chapters ties a real Omani hazard to a real NASA mission: wadi floods (GPM), algal blooms (PACE), farm heatwaves (SMAP) and dust storms (Terra and Aqua), ending with real NASA imagery of Oman. A rumour check teaches media literacy: players can only verify a viral message with the instruments they chose, and “I can’t confirm” is often the smartest answer.

Nominal runs in any phone browser with no installation, and supports Arabic. It shows young people that satellites help predict, warn and respond, and helps them think critically about trade-offs and misinformation.
details:
What it does and how it works
Nominal is a story-driven web game about designing a space mission. Players help Noor, a 13-year-old girl from Sur, Oman, build a satellite for her school’s competition, guided by her grandfather Jaddi Salim, a former dhow sailor who navigated by the stars. Each of the four chapters starts with a real Omani hazard that affects Noor’s family: wadi flash floods, harmful algal blooms near Sur, a heatwave on a farm in Al Batinah, and a shamal dust storm.

Players get 100 budget points to choose a rocket, scientific instruments, an orbit, solar panels and an antenna. Every part costs points, adds mass and uses power, and the game shows what each choice rules out (opportunity cost). A launch check cancels any design that is over budget, too heavy for the rocket, or short on power. Once in orbit, players respond to events based on real space operations, such as micrometeoroid strikes, solar storms, space debris warnings and ground station outages, where spare power and budget reserves matter. A rumour then spreads in the family group chat, and players can only check it using the instruments they chose. If they lack the right data, the correct answer is “I can’t confirm.” Each chapter ends with a score, what the player gave up, and the real NASA mission that does the same job (GPM, PACE, SMAP, Terra and Aqua), shown with real NASA imagery of Oman.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Teaches real engineering trade-offs (mass, power, data, orbit, cost) without needing a physics background.
  • Builds media literacy: players learn to check claims against evidence and to admit when they don’t have enough data.
  • Corrects common misconceptions with myth vs. fact cards, for example that space is freezing, or that satellites can stop storms. In reality, satellites help predict, warn and respond.
  • Connects space science to local issues students recognise, and introduces real NASA Earth-observation missions.
  • Gives teachers a ready classroom activity. Teacher (demo) mode makes events predictable, so a whole class plays the same round.

Tools and technologies
Python and Streamlit for the web app; JSON files for all game data, story text and translations, so new missions can be added without new code; SVG graphics generated in Python for the live satellite drawing, scenes and mission patches; Streamlit’s AppTest and Playwright for automated playthroughs and screenshot checks on phone and laptop sizes; GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud for free hosting. NASA mission information and imagery come from NASA sources (GPM, PACE, SMAP, Terra/Aqua MODIS, ASTER, Earth Observatory). We used Claude, an AI assistant, as a coding and design assistant, while our team set the direction, made the design and content decisions, and reviewed the science and the Arabic.

What makes it creative
Instead of a quiz, it’s a story: design choices become story choices, and their consequences reach Noor’s family. The visual style is rooted in Gulf heritage: Al Sadu weaving patterns, Omani forts and souqs, and a satellite “woven” in Sadu style. Jaddi Salim links traditional star navigation with modern Earth observation. The rumour mechanic ties misinformation directly to design: what you can verify depends on what you built.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific validity: every part has a fact card with real values, the simplifications are honest, and we corrected an early idea (dust covering solar panels in orbit) that wasn’t physically possible.
  • Game balance: we tested all 2,214 possible designs per mission to make sure the trade-offs are real and no mission is trivial.
  • Accessibility: it works in any phone browser with no installation or accounts, the wording is simplified for younger readers, and it has an Arabic version with right-to-left layout (Flood Watch fully translated).
  • Cultural relevance: Omani places, families and everyday language.
  • Reliability for live use: bundled fonts and images so it works on weak Wi-Fi, and a predictable demo mode.
